info.title: apicraft API
info.summary: GitHub release API on your own GitHub token: version checks, downloads, changelogs and a tracked-repository list.
info.description:
Check whether a version is outdated against the newest GitHub release of any repository your token can read. Built for the storytold Craft applications behind ArtCraft, but it works for every public repo.

**How it works:** create a free account at `/login/`, save your own GitHub token on the account page, then call the API with your personal key (`ac_...`) in `Authorization: Bearer`. Every request runs on *your* GitHub token and quota; the server never spends its own.

**Authorize:** press *Authorize* and paste your `ac_` key. Responses carry `X-RateLimit-*` and `X-RateLimit-Policy` headers, an `X-Request-ID` and (on JSON GETs) an `ETag`. Every error has the same JSON shape with a stable `error` code, a `hint` and sometimes an `action`. Create one named *automation key* per script on the dashboard (read-only or full). Live service state is at `/status/`.

get.description: Public. Tells the login page whether emailed codes are on, and where the Buy me a coffee pop-up points.

post.description:
One call for both. If the email has an account, the password is checked and you are logged in; if not, an account is created with that password and you are logged in. The password is checked before anything is emailed. One mailbox, one account: `+tags`, upper case and (for Gmail) dots do not make a new address.

**With email codes on**, the first call (no `code`) checks the password and mails a 6-digit code (`code_sent: true`); repeat the call with `code` to finish. Calling again without `code` after the cooldown sends a fresh one. Codes expire after 10 minutes, work once and allow 5 attempts.
Emails a 6-digit code to reset the password. The answer is identical whether or not the address has an account. Answers 503 while email codes are switched off.

post.summary: Forgot Password: Set a New One
post.description: Checks the emailed code, sets the new password, signs out every other session and logs you in. Answers 503 while email codes are switched off.

get.summary: Get User Profile & Active API Key
get.description: Returns the signed-in user's email, API key, limits, whether a GitHub token is saved, and 7-day usage telemetry.
Tells you whether you saved a GitHub token, whether GitHub still accepts it and how many requests per hour it has left. The token itself is never returned.

put.description: GitHub is asked first and the token is refused unless it works. It is then stored AES-256-GCM encrypted and every API call you make runs on it, under your own 5,000 requests per hour. Fine-grained tokens with no permissions are enough for public repositories.

delete.description: Deletes the saved token. API calls that need GitHub stop working until you save a new one.

post.description: Immediately revokes the previous API key and issues a new dual-animal API key with an embedded CRC32 checksum.

get.description: Browser session only. Extra API keys for scripts and CI, each with its own name and access (read-only or full). Only the start of each key is shown; the key itself is shown once, when it is created. All keys share your account's rate limits and your GitHub token.

post.description: Browser session only. Creates a named key. `read` can call every GET endpoint and the batch check; `full` can also add, change and remove tracked repositories. The key is returned once and cannot be shown again. Delete it any time to revoke it.

put.description: Browser session only. Rename a key, change its access, set or remove its expiry and its daily cap. The secret does not change; use rotate for that.

delete.description: Browser session only. The key stops working within a few seconds.

post.description: Browser session only. Issues a new secret for the same key (name, access, expiry and daily cap stay) and the old secret stops working at once. Shown once.
Destroys the active server-side session and instructs the browser to delete the session cookie.
Browser session only. Needs the current password. Every session is signed out and this browser gets a fresh one. Your API key does not change.

Browser session only. Needs your password. One mailbox, one account: an address that belongs to another account is refused. While email codes are on, the first call mails a code to the NEW address and you repeat the call with `code` to finish. Other sessions are signed out; this browser gets a fresh one. Your API key does not change.
Browser session only. Ends every session on every device, including this one. Your API key keeps working.

get.description: Which of the three modules (Craft Watch, Contributors, CraftSuite tracker) are on, whether they can run, when they last ran and how much data they hold. The owner of the server switches them on the Admin page. Includes the credits.

One entry per app: latest release, the update verdict (green, yellow, red, grey), activity numbers (the *alive* meter), advisories, OpenSSF Scorecard and, when the CraftSuite module is on, the readiness percentage. Served from the collector's data, so it costs no GitHub request.

Verdict with its evidence, the four stat cards, recent merged pull requests, releases, published advisories, open problems and most wanted features (by thumbs-up), the 30-day history and the report spike check for the newest release.

get.description: Lists the files attached to the newest release, each tagged with the OS and CPU it is for. Pass `os` (and optionally `arch`) to get a `best` match: an exact CPU match first, then a universal build.

Collects the notes of every release newer than `current`, so a jump from 18.2.0 to 19.0.0 does not hide what 18.3 and 18.4 changed. `breaking_changes` is true when any of the notes mention breaking changes, migrations or deprecations.
Stars, forks, open issues, language, licence, last push and the newest release in one call.
Recently updated pull requests, so you can see what is in progress before it ships.
Recently updated issues. GitHub mixes pull requests into its issue list; they are filtered out here.
Compares two refs. By default it compares the latest release tag with the default branch, so `ahead_by` is the number of commits merged since the last release.

get.summary: Your Tracked Repositories With Current Status
get.description: The repositories you track, each checked against its newest release on your own GitHub token. Works for private repositories your token can read. Filter with `group` and `only` (`outdated`, `current` or `error`).

parameters.name: only

schema.description: Only outdated, up to date or failing repositories
schema.title: Only

parameters.description: Only outdated, up to date or failing repositories

post.description: Tracks a repository together with the version you run. Posting it again updates version, label and group. Per-account cap: 50 (owner 200). A repository your token cannot see is refused. Needs a `full` key or the website.

put.description: Adds or updates up to 200 repositories in one call. With `replace: true` every tracked repository that is not in `items` is removed, so a file in your repository can be the single source of truth. Repositories that fail the GitHub check are listed in `rejected` and the rest is stored. A call costs one request per 5 repositories. Needs a `full` key or the website.

get.summary: One-Look Summary for Scripts and CI
get.description: Counts instead of a list: how many tracked repositories are up to date, outdated or failing, per group, plus the outdated ones. `all_current` is true when nothing needs attention, so a pipeline can gate on a single field.
Aggregates tracked repositories by custom track / environment (prod, staging, tools, etc.), providing update counts, health status, and repository lists for automated pipeline gating.

post.summary: Mark All Repositories in a Track as Updated
post.description: Sets current version = latest for all outdated repositories in the specified track/group. Ideal for CI/CD post-deployment hooks to mark an entire environment current in one request.

get.description: Designed for CI/CD gates and health check scripts. Returns `exit_code: 0` if all tracked repositories in the given track/group are up to date, or `exit_code: 1` if updates are available or errors occurred, along with the list of outdated repositories.
Exports your tracked repositories in multiple formats: `json`, `csv`, `yaml`, `markdown`, or `matrix` (GitHub Actions workflow strategy matrix).

post.description: Sets the version you run to the newest release, for the moment after a deployment. Needs a `full` key or the website.

delete.description: Needs a `full` key or the website.

get.description: Returns live GitHub API rate limit metrics (5,000 req/hr authenticated or 60 req/hr anonymous), Apicraft account tier limits, and secondary rate limit avoidance guidance per GitHub best practices.
Returns verified guidance based on GitHub official documentation on Personal Access Tokens, least-privilege fine-grained permissions, token revocation triggers, and rate limit architectures.
The newest version of each repository shown on the homepage. Refreshed in the background every 30 minutes and served from memory, so it needs no key and costs no GitHub request.
Live state of the website, API, account database, sign-in, GitHub connection and homepage data, one uptime bar per day, and recent incidents. This is what the /status/ page shows. No key needed.

get.description: Liveness probe for load balancers and uptime monitors. Not rate limited, no key needed. For the full picture see `/public/status`.
Your limits, the remaining quota in the tightest window, the reset countdown and your 7-day request history.

Every API call your account made is stored (time, endpoint, query, status, duration) for 90 days; the daily totals are kept for good. Returns totals, a bar per day, your most called endpoints, status code counts and the newest calls. `via=apikey` shows only calls made with your key, `via=session` only what the website did for you. `format=csv` downloads the raw rows of the window (up to 100,000) instead. Reading the history is not itself logged.
